items.followUp: Compare the structure and function of capillaries and veins.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the direction in which blood flows in arteries and veins.
rubric.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry blood towards the heart.
rubric.how: Award when both directions are correctly compared.

rubric.why: Compares the walls of the two vessels.
rubric.description: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls; veins have thinner walls.
rubric.how: Award for a correct contrast in wall structure or thickness.

rubric.why: Compares the lumen sizes, an important structural difference.
rubric.description: Arteries have a narrower lumen; veins have a wider lumen.
rubric.how: Award for correctly comparing lumen size.

rubric.why: Recognises a functional or structural distinction related to blood pressure and flow.
rubric.description: Blood flows through arteries under higher pressure; veins have valves to prevent backflow.

modelAnswer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, while veins carry blood towards the heart.
Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls and a narrow lumen; veins have thinner walls and a wider lumen.
Blood flows through arteries under high pressure; blood in veins is at lower pressure.
Veins have valves to prevent backflow; arteries generally do not have valves along their length.

items.followUp: Define an ecosystem and name two components of an ecosystem.

rubric.why: Defines the biosphere as the region of Earth in which life occurs.
rubric.description: The biosphere is the zone of life on Earth, where organisms live.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the biosphere as Earth's life-supporting zone.

rubric.why: Shows the extent of the biosphere across Earth's environments.
rubric.description: It includes life-supporting regions of land, water and the lower atmosphere.
rubric.how: Award for naming at least two of these environments or equivalent wording.

modelAnswer: The biosphere is the zone of life on Earth—the part of Earth where organisms live.
It includes life-supporting regions of land, water and the lower atmosphere.

items.followUp: What is an organ? Explain how cells are organised to form a tissue.

rubric.why: States what a cell is in relation to living organisms.
rubric.description: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of an organism.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the cell as the basic unit of life or structure and function.

rubric.why: Defines a tissue by its cells and their shared function.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a particular function.
rubric.how: Award when both a group of similar cells and a shared function are conveyed.

modelAnswer: Cell level: a cell is the basic structural and functional unit of an organism.
Tissue level: a tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a particular function.

items.followUp: What are qualitative observations? Give one example.

rubric.why: Explains that quantitative observations use measurements or numerical data.
rubric.description: Quantitative observations are observations expressed in numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning numerical or measured data.

rubric.why: Provides a suitable numerical example of a measured observation.
rubric.description: Example: a plant is 10 cm tall.
rubric.how: Award for a relevant example that includes a quantity or measurement.

modelAnswer: Quantitative observations are observations expressed as numbers or measurements.
Example: a plant is 10 cm tall.
